content: Homeopathy is a type of complementary or alternative medicine that is often promoted as a safe and effective treatment option for both children and adults. Within the United Kingdom, it is estimated that 1.9% of the adult population uses homeopathy, while approximately 11% of children under the age of 16 have used it. There has been growing interest in exploring homeopathy as a non-pharmacological treatment for attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), particularly as an alternative to stimulant medications like Ritalin. The practice of homeopathy is based on the principle of like cures like, which involves using highly diluted natural or synthetic substances. This approach emphasizes the unique characteristics of each patient’s symptoms and experiences to guide the selection of an individualized treatment. The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of homeopathy as a treatment for ADHD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted, covering their inception up to March 2006. The databases included CENTRAL, MEDLINE, AMED, BIOSIS, CISCOM, CINAHL, Dissertation Abstracts, the European Committee for Homeopathy thesis database (ECH), EMBASE, ERIC, HomInform (Glasgow Homeopathic Hospital Library), LILACS, PsycINFO, Science Citation Index, SIGLE, GIRI (International Congress on Ultra-Low Doses), and Liga Medicorum Homeopathica Internationalis. Experts in the field were also contacted to identify ongoing or unpublished research. The selection criteria for the study included all research where individualized, clinical, or formula-based homeopathy was used to treat participants diagnosed with ADHD or hyperkinetic disorder (HKD). Participants had to be randomly or quasi-randomly assigned to either a homeopathy treatment group or a control group. Control groups could include those receiving no treatment, wait-list controls, placebo homeopathy, standard medication, or educational or behavioral interventions. Data from four eligible studies, involving a total of 168 participants, were extracted and analyzed using RevMan software. The results were synthesized, and effect sizes were calculated where possible. These findings were presented in both graphical and narrative formats. In cases where effect size calculations were not feasible, only narrative descriptions were provided. The main results of the analysis indicated that the forms of homeopathy evaluated so far do not demonstrate significant treatment effects for the global symptoms of ADHD, including core symptoms such as inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity. Additionally, no significant effects were observed for related outcomes, such as anxiety. The authors concluded that there is currently limited evidence to support the efficacy of homeopathy as a treatment for ADHD. They recommend the development of optimized treatment protocols before conducting further randomized controlled trials.
